Hold Before You Step

The Information Requirement of In-Place Push Recovery on Force-Sensorless Humanoids

Jeonghyeon Kim1Jaesang Kim2Shinsuk Park1

1 Korea University  ·  2 University College London

TLDRA humanoid without force sensors can absorb a push with its feet planted, but only if it learns about the push within about ten milliseconds.

Abstract

Holding a push in place, instead of stepping, preserves a humanoid’s task stance, but only if the push is recognised in time. Without force or torque sensors the push is known only through an estimate that arrives late and with error. We measure how much lateness and error a hold tolerates, choose an estimate that meets this requirement, and design the controller’s signal paths by it. The controller recovers as often as a stepping baseline with 49 % fewer steps.

Video

From the problem to the hardware tests in 55 seconds. Robot scenes are rendered in Viser on the MuJoCo G1 model.

Problem

A robot without force sensors does not see the push. It sees an estimate of it, which is late by L and wrong by σ. The hold or step decision runs on that estimate. The question is how large L and σ may be before a push that could be held ends in a step.

Method

Three parts. The information requirement is measured by feeding a fixed controller the true push, delayed and corrupted on purpose. It selects the estimate, which must be fast at low noise, and it sets how the controller filters each use of that estimate.

push forcerequirementsensor signalestimateholdstepactuation

(A) Requirement from a fixed controller

The hold decision loses pushes within tens of milliseconds. At a 10 ms delay 10 of 12 are still held, at 20 ms only 3. The loss follows a pendulum model, and actuation delay spends the same budget as information delay. Slow errors of 30 N pass. Errors of 20 N on the time scale of the push do not.

(B) Estimate from the pelvis IMU

A momentum observer differentiates a base velocity reconstructed from leg kinematics, which is noisy at low latency. This estimate measures the base acceleration with the pelvis IMU and solves the base and leg rows of the floating base model for the push wrench. It needs the torque of the 12 leg joints only. On the real G1 it followed a load cell by 29 ms, against 57 ms for a momentum observer.

(C) Hold layer on a stepping controller

The estimate reaches the hold layer by three paths. The decision path is unfiltered because latency comes first. The force bound takes a median to reject spikes. The feedforward keeps its filter. The stepping baseline stays underneath as the fallback.

Results

Simulation, 80 paired runs with pushes of 50 to 80 N. All rows share the plant, the stance controller and the pushes. They differ only in the step decision and its information.

65 vs 62runs recovered, ours against the stepping baseline. The preregistered criterion is met.
49 % fewer stepswith 30 pushes held in place against none.
96 % less displacementof the base on holdable pushes both recovered, with 69 % less leg work.

Hardware

A real G1 in a safety gantry, pushed by hand through a load cell sampled at 7.5 kHz and logged on the robot’s clock.

The same controller with steps enabled, with the hold layer off (stepping baseline) and on (ours), under lateral hand pushes of about 40 N. Load-cell force, hold mode and foot swing are taken from the robot’s logs and synchronised to the video. Selected illustrative trials; the registered comparison is below.

Hold layer on vs. off. In a registered test with steps disabled, the same controller with and without the hold layer received ascending series of shoulder-height lateral pushes, 12 blocks each. Ours held 42 of 49 pushes of 40–80 N; without the hold layer the controller held none (0 of 6 in that range, 0 of 24 overall), unloading a foot from 22 N (Fisher p < 0.0001).

Holding in place. With our controller in command and steps disabled, 21 of 22 lateral pushes of 26–59 N were held without a step under a registered outcome rule. The hold mode started 69 ms (median) after the load cell crossed 25 N, a time that includes the gradual rise of the hand push and the estimate’s delay.

Estimators. 71 hand pushes with the estimators running in shadow, computed but not commanded.
